title: Bitcoin ETF Inflows Stall After $1.7 Billion Burst: Will Demand Return?
summary: Bitcoin ETF inflows have totaled just $232 million in 13 sessions since a $1.7 billion burst. Can buyers return?
content:
US spot Bitcoin (BTC) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have added only about $232 million over 13 sessions. Bitcoin ETF inflows totaled $1.7 billion across September 21 and 22, then went quiet.

Bitcoin's price recovered to above $83,000 overnight while US-listed funds were not trading, so ETF buyers have not confirmed the move. Monday's flow data will show whether they follow.

Data tracker SoSoValue shows the funds drew $999 million on September 21 and $714.8 million on September 22. Cumulative inflows hit $56.87 billion by the end of that second day.

However, an inflow streak ended on September 30 with a $148.7 million outflow, and ETF demand has faded since.

Brief relief followed, with $102.7 million entering on October 1 and $189.8 million on October 2.

Then the two largest outflows of the past 13 sessions hit on October 7 and 8, totaling $731.2 million.

Total net assets fell from $110.77 billion on October 5 to $105.84 billion on October 9. Net outflows over that span totaled $591 million, so lower prices likely drove most of the drop.

Friday's $21.13 million inflow ended a two-day outflow run. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) took in $22.38 million, more than the day's net total.

In contrast, Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC) lost $3.58 million. Nine of the 12 funds posted zero flows.

IBIT alone holds $66.3 billion of the $105.84 billion in total net assets, about 63%. Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC), meanwhile, has recorded $27.94 billion in cumulative net outflows.

Friday's $1.44 billion in total value traded was the lowest of the 13 sessions. October 8 had marked the highest, at $3.18 billion.

A Fear and Greed sentiment reading of 39 sits in the fear zone, according to CoinGecko.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs hold 6.38% of Bitcoin's market value, according to SoSoValue, so their flows gauge institutional demand. A rally without them would need other buyers. Earlier this month, Glassnode data tied a pullback to weak trading volume.

title: Solana ETFs End a 14-Week Buying Streak With Their Largest Weekly Exit
summary: Solana ETFs lost $24.8 million last week, ending a 14-week inflow streak, while XRP ETFs extended their run.
content:
US spot Solana (SOL) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) lost $24.8 million in the week ending October 9. It was their largest weekly outflow since launch in October 2025 and ended 14 straight inflow weeks.

Just 2 weeks earlier, the funds drew $188.2 million, their second-biggest week on record. Inflows then slowed to $2.4 million in the week ending October 2.

According to SoSoValue data, the previous weekly record was an $8.9 million outflow in the week ending February 6. Last week's exit was almost 3 times that size.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

Bitcoin (BTC) ETFs shed $681.1 million in the same week, while Ethereum (ETH) ETFs lost $542.1 million. Ethereum funds closed the week on a ninth straight outflow day, BeInCrypto reported.

Zcash (ZEC) and Hyperliquid (HYPE) ETFs also posted outflows of $30.7 million and $9.4 million, respectively.

Net assets in the Solana funds fell 8.9% over the week, from $1.90 billion to $1.73 billion. The outflow accounts for only about $25 million of that $170 million decline. The rest largely reflects SOL's price slide over the same period.

SOL fell 10.25% during the trading week before recording modest gains over the weekend. The altcoin traded at $111.53 at press time, up 1.45% over the past 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto Markets data.

The next weekly print, covering trading through October 16, will show whether fund buyers returned after the price drop.

Meanwhile, spot XRP (XRP) ETFs moved in the opposite direction, drawing $11.3 million over the same week. The inflow extended their streak to 13 consecutive weeks.

Their last outflow week ended July 10. In contrast, other major ETFs all posted net outflows last week.

The buying held up even as XRP fell 8.2% during the week. Cumulative net inflows into XRP ETFs reached a record $1.80 billion. Net assets, however, stood lower at $1.57 billion.

Even so, Solana and XRP ETFs have each drawn more net money in 2026 than spot Bitcoin ETFs. Since January 1, Solana funds have attracted $816.8 million and XRP funds $635.5 million, against $494.1 million for Bitcoin.

title: IREN's Mystery Customer Is Anthropic? Fresh Buzz Pushes Stock Higher

content:

title: Treasury Yields Are Now Above 5%. Here's Why That's Bearish For Bitcoin.
summary: Investors shouldn't conflate the devaluation of fiat currencies with rising Treasury yields.
content:
The 10-Year Treasury yield recently hit 5.3%, its highest level since 2007. As a result, issuers of CDs, bonds, and other fixed-income investments will need to raise their yields to stay competitive. That shift could draw investors away from stocks and other riskier investments.

Some investors might argue that Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is immune to that shift because it's becoming a safe-haven hedge against the debasement of fiat currencies. But at $84,000, Bitcoin remains about 33% below its all-time high of $126,000 from last October. Let's see why higher yields are weighing down Bitcoin -- and why it might bounce back if those yields decline.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Bitcoin is mined using the energy-intensive proof-of-work ( PoW ) consensus mechanism, which relies on powerful computing hardware to solve cryptographic puzzles. But every four years, a scheduled "halving" halves those rewards, making it even harder to mine Bitcoin profitably.

More than 20 million of Bitcoin's maximum supply of 21 million tokens have already been mined, but its increasing difficulty will prevent its last token from being mined until 2140. That scarcity makes it more comparable to gold than many other cryptocurrencies, so it's often considered a hedge against inflation and the devaluation of the U.S. dollar.

However, rising Treasury yields also usually drive investors away from gold. While gold might be a good hedge against a weakening dollar, rising yields actually strengthen the U.S. dollar. As that happens, it makes more sense for investors to shift from gold toward low-risk CDs, Treasuries, bonds, and other fixed-income investments that pay guaranteed interest. At the same time, rising borrowing costs will prevent investors from taking on riskier, leveraged bets and drive them to liquidate more volatile investments to fund their fixed-income purchases.

Bitcoin, as "digital gold," is exposed to the same headwinds. Many institutional investors will also rotate out of Bitcoin ETFs -- which provide exposure to Bitcoin without crypto wallets and keys -- as Treasury yields rise. So while Bitcoin and gold still might be good long-term bets against the U.S. dollar and other fiat currencies, they won't bounce back unless the Treasury yields cool off and risk-seeking investors return to the market.

I'm still bullish on Bitcoin's long-term growth potential, since monetary expansion policies will inevitably debase fiat currencies. But investors shouldn't conflate that debasement with the near-term pressures of rising interest rates and Treasury yields. Those challenges could prevent Bitcoin from revisiting its all-time highs for the foreseeable future.

title: Bots are Changing South Korea’s Famous Bitcoin Price Gap
summary: South Korea’s Kimchi Premium is no longer a simple story of human traders chasing price gaps: all you need to know.
content:
Bitcoin can cost more in South Korea than it does almost anywhere else. For years, traders chased that gap for profit. Now, automated trading is making the race faster, while strict banking rules still decide who can take part.

The price difference, known as the Kimchi Premium, was once a popular sign of Korean investors rushing into crypto. Its meaning is becoming harder to read.

The trade sounds simple: buy Bitcoin cheaply abroad, transfer it to a Korean exchange, and sell it for more.

But South Korea restricts cross-border money transfers. Traders cannot always move their profits back overseas freely. That helps explain why the premium can survive even when everyone sees it.

Historically, a widening gap often signaled strong local demand. Investors watched it for clues that retail speculation was heating up.

Evidence suggests some traders have already automated the process.

A June 2026 study examined 16,228 arbitrage transactions between Binance and Bithumb. Researchers found 96% took place within five-minute intervals, pointing to possible automated trading.

That does not prove AI agents control the market. But it shows how difficult it can be for manual traders to compete with software.

Korea's tighter investor-protection rules add another obstacle. Exchanges face greater oversight, while restrictions on moving money across borders still limit who can exploit the spread.

The gap can widen when Korean buyers get aggressive. It can also reflect slower selling, currency changes, or shifts in local market sentiment.

Meanwhile, retail demand remains substantial. Chainalysis estimates South Korea's crypto economy at $449 billion over its latest study period, with investors particularly interested in AI-linked tokens.

Proposed won-backed stablecoins could eventually make settlement easier, if regulators permit them.

For investors, a rising Kimchi Premium still matters. But treating it as automatic proof of a buying frenzy risks missing what is happening behind the prices.

title: Bitcoin Could Be Entering a New Bull Market Despite Latest Sell-Off
summary: BloFin Research says Bitcoin's new bull market remains intact despite the latest sell-off, as historical data suggests its boom-and-bust cycles are weakening.
content:
Despite the market dip and liquidations over the past week, Bitcoin has seemingly entered a bull market, as the analysis of its 50-week moving average shows.

BloFin Research argues that Bitcoin's traditional four-year boom-and-bust cycle is gradually losing strength. Future rallies could deliver smaller gains, followed by shorter and less severe downturns.

The strongest evidence comes from Bitcoin's recovery above its 50-week moving average, a technical indicator that previously signaled bull-market transitions in 2015, 2019 and 2023.

Bitcoin reclaimed this level near $78,800 in September. It subsequently traded above $86,000 in early October.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin's MVRV ratio, which compares its current market value with the average price investors paid for their coins, moved above its annual average.

As of October 11, MVRV stood near 1.54, above its 365-day average of 1.44. This suggests the longer-term recovery remains intact despite recent selling.

It means Bitcoin's market strength is improving, a signal that has previously appeared during the early stages of bull markets.

BloFin's most significant finding concerns the declining severity of Bitcoin's market cycles.

Bitcoin fell approximately 53% from its October 2025 peak of $124,824 to $58,525 in June 2026.

Previous bear markets were considerably worse:

Bull-market gains have also narrowed. Bitcoin's trough-to-peak returns have declined from roughly 530 times in its earliest cycle to eight times in the most recent one.

If June remains the bottom, the latest bear market lasted approximately eight months, compared with 12–13 months historically.

BloFin Research attributes much of this change to longer-term ownership. In September, approximately 16.64 million BTC, or 83% of circulating supply, had remained unmoved for at least 155 days.

Meanwhile, US spot Bitcoin ETFs held around 1.3 million BTC on October 2. Public companies owned another 1.29 million BTC.

Together, ETFs and corporate treasuries controlled approximately 13% of circulating Bitcoin.

However, last week's $679 million ETF outflow shows that institutional demand can still weaken sharply during market stress.

Bitcoin was trading around $83,000 on October 11, still above the September moving-average breakout level and well above its June low.

The four-year cycle also remains visible. Bitcoin peaked roughly 18 months after the April 2024 halving, consistent with historical patterns.

For traders, a sustained move below the current 50-week moving average would weaken the bullish signal. A break beneath $58,525 would challenge the proposed cycle bottom.

For now, Bitcoin's longer-term recovery indicators remain positive. The recent ETF withdrawals show why the transition toward a more stable market could still involve sharp corrections.

title: Peter Schiff Says Bitcoin Surprised Him By Holding Gains As He Still Expects New Lows
summary: Peter Schiff is against a government-backed strategic Bitcoin reserve.
content:
Peter Schiff said he's surprised gold surrendered its post-buyback gains while Bitcoin held onto them.

He still expects Bitcoin to test new lows once the tech-led stock rally stalls.

He warned that the Nov. 3 midterms could turn Washington against Bitcoin.

Gold advocate Peter Schiff admitted he's surprised Bitcoin (BTC) has held onto gains that gold has given back, but still expects the cryptocurrency to fall to new lows.

Schiff made the comments in an interview with Scott Melker on his podcast, The Wolf Of All Streets, published on Sunday. Both assets surged after the Treasury announced that it would double its long-dated bond buybacks to at least $4 billion per operation.

Bitcoin was trading at about $60,000 before that statement and is now close to $85,000, Schiff added. But on the news, gold shot up to around $4,700, then has since cooled off to around $4,000, he added. "I do expect it to make new lows. I just would have thought it would have happened already," he said.

He said that Bitcoin is riding the same technology rally that has boosted the most large-cap stocks. Schiff said that he expects it to fall when the rally fades.

Bitcoin's price was trading around $83,790, up 1% in the last 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC remained in the 'bearish' zone, accompanied by 'low' chatter levels over the past day.

Schiff also said Strategy (MSTR), the largest corporate holder of BTC, sold Bitcoin earlier this year as part of a plan to pay dividends on its preferred stock. As of now, it has bought back some of its Stretch preferred stock (STRC) and started buying Bitcoins again in small amounts, which he called "it's all window dressing."

According to Schiff, the midterm elections on November 3 could have an impact on Bitcoin. He claimed that Republicans have made Bitcoin a partisan issue, whereas Democrats see it as a source of funding and votes for their opponents.

"Bitcoin is a Republican thing now," Schiff said. He predicted a Democratic Congress would target the industry. "Washington is going to be more of an enemy than a friend when it comes to Bitcoin," he said.

Adding to that, Schiff said he doesn't want the government to back Bitcoin through a strategic reserve. "I want the government to stay neutral," he said.

title: Sui Soars 48% in Just One Month: Could It Be the Next Solana?
summary: Sui just posted one of crypto's most eye-catching monthly gains, and a new Bitcoin lending system on its network is drawing comparisons to Solana's early rise. But a closer look at the numbers tells a more complicated story.
content:
Sui surged 48% in one month fueled by Hashi, a system letting institutions borrow against Bitcoin without selling it.

Sui trades 80% below its all-time high and would need a 100x price increase to match Solana's current price.

Sui's rally likely reflects broad altcoin market appetite rather than organic demand, and Hashi has yet to publish any adoption metrics.

Crypto enthusiasts are buzzing that Sui (CRYPTO:SUI) might be the next Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) after a remarkable 48.6% gain over the last month. This surge coincided with the emergence of Hashi, a new system on Sui that allows institutions to borrow against Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC). A strong price move, combined with an innovative use case, has reignited comparisons to Solana.

However, the recent rally has slowed down. As of October 11, 2026, Sui trades at $1.10, down 7.2% over the past week. Sui is a layer-1 blockchain, meaning it is a foundational network that processes transactions and hosts applications directly, with its coin used to pay transaction fees.

So what would it mean for Sui to become "the next Solana"?

While 24/7 Wall St. has not independently verified Hashi's details, reports indicate it lets institutions raise cash against their Bitcoin without selling. The process involves locking Bitcoin in a multisignature vault on the Bitcoin main chain—a secure wallet that requires multiple approvals before anyone can move any coins. In exchange, the institution receives a corresponding token on Sui, allowing them to take out a loan, similar to how homeowners borrow against their property.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

This approach is appealing because selling Bitcoin can trigger tax liabilities and eliminate the possibility of future gains. Loans let Bitcoin holders keep ownership while accessing cash. There seems to be a strong demand for these loans. In an October 2026 episode of The Pomp Podcast , a guest from a crypto finance platform mentioned that their fastest-growing segment involves borrowing against cryptocurrencies.

However, taking a Hashi loan comes with risks. A Bitcoin holder's security depends solely on Bitcoin's price, while a borrower using Hashi also depends on Sui's functionality and the vault system's integrity. Crypto-backed loans become riskier as collateral value declines. As Hashi has yet to publish usage or loan metrics, it's uncertain how much traction it has gained.

Bitcoin lending gives Sui a unique selling proposition, and Sui is already part of the CME Emerging Crypto Index, a benchmark tracking a select group of cryptocurrencies. Still, Sui requires proven user engagement to back up that pitch.

Sui has clearly outperformed Solana over the past month, gaining 48.6% compared to Solana's modest 9.6% increase. Both cryptocurrencies fell in the past week, but Solana's decline was slightly steeper.

On the downside, Solana has shown better resilience relative to its all-time high, trading 62.7% below its peak, while Sui is down 79.5%. Thus, Sui holders are still facing a significant challenge to recover.

When we talk about "the next Solana," we mean matching Solana's price, which is currently 100 times Sui's. For Sui to reach Solana's price point, it would need to increase a hundredfold. The data does not suggest that this will occur anytime soon. Instead of focusing solely on price, it's essential to assess demand.

The key question is whether Sui can capture a meaningful portion of the demand that Solana currently serves, attracting traders, app developers, and institutions seeking a fast, cost-effective network. To achieve this, Sui must maintain consistent developer activity, secure ongoing institutional investment, and have applications that keep users engaged after the initial rally fades.

A single month of growth isn't enough to establish a trend. Sui's rise happened during a market phase when traders shifted funds from larger cryptocurrencies to smaller, riskier options. Therefore, much of Sui's success likely stems from broader market risk appetite rather than independent demand for Sui itself.

Three indicators could strengthen the argument for Sui as a serious contender. First, Hashi should release user adoption figures; without solid usage data, it remains merely a concept. title: Oil Traders Are About to Test Trump’s Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire Claim, But Bitcoin Reacted First
summary: Bitcoin rose on Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire claim. Oil futures reopen next to test a truce neither side confirmed.
content:
Bitcoin (BTC) rose to $84,000 on Sunday after President Donald Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed the deal.

Oil futures have been closed since Friday. When they reopen Sunday evening in New York, energy traders get their first chance to price a truce that rests on a single post.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that both sides had agreed and warned them not to break it. He gave no terms, start time, or way to check compliance.

Crypto markets moved anyway. Both Bitcoin and Ethereum prices rose in the immediate aftermath of the news, albeit modest gains.

The rise hit traders betting on a fall. A liquidation happens when an exchange force-closes a borrowed bet that has lost too much.

CoinGlass data showed $70 million in short bets wiped out over four hours. Long liquidations totaled only $6.9 million.

Shorts made up 97.1% of the $22.29 million liquidated on Bitcoin in that window. The reaction contrasts with June, when BTC barely moved on the Senate's Iran vote.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the announcement was "news for me." He then set out his terms.

"If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it," Axios reported, citing Zelensky.

Still, it is important to note that the EU is preparing additional funding for Ukrainian drones and missiles, even as Zelensky mulls a possible ceasefire on energy infrastructure.

Moscow had not commented by press time. On October 8, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia saw no point in a sector-only ceasefire, reported the Kyiv Independent.

Trump made a similar claim in September. Neither side confirmed it, and both kept striking energy sites.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the US crude benchmark, last settled at $91.66 a barrel. Brent, the global benchmark, closed at $104.42.

The war with Iran has already pushed fuel prices higher, as BeInCrypto tracked when oil passed $110 in April. Trump has since eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports and pressed Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries.

Bitcoin has already voted on the ceasefire. Oil, the market most exposed to it, votes next.

title: Ledger Wallet Spy Implant Scare Spreads To Europe As Crypto Losses Top $86M: Report
summary: Mark Karpelès confirmed the implant and said it reads the seed phrase off the device’s screen, the set of words that can unlock a wallet’s funds.
content:
A user said on Sunday that a Ledger device bought from an official European reseller had a spy implant, suggesting a scare that began in Asia may have spread.

Ledger confirmed that at least one affected device had an unauthorized implant. It traced the cases to Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, which has stopped all hardware wallet sales.

Trackers estimate losses at $72 million to more than $86 million across Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron. More than $10 million has been frozen so far.

A Ledger hardware wallet scare that began with Asian users losing funds has reportedly spread to Europe after a user said a device bought from an official European reseller contained the same spy implant.

According to Johannes, a well-known crypto twitter user who calls out bad actors, the device had been bought in a store a couple of weeks ago. "PSA the ledger incident isn't limited to Asia," he wrote on Sunday.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

He shared photos showing extra wires inside the device that a genuine Ledger hardware doesn't have. Johannes said the European device never sent funds to an attacker. He said it's unclear whether the implant failed or the attackers were waiting. He urged anyone who didn't buy directly from Ledger's online store to open the device and check it themselves.

Karpelès Lab CEO Mark Karpelès, who has been opening up tampered Ledger devices, confirmed the find. "Another spy implant confirmed," he said on X. He added that it looked like an earlier version of the implant he is studying, "meaning there were more iterations."

A hardware wallet is a small device that stores a user's crypto keys offline. When a user sets one up, the screen shows a seed phrase, a list of words that can restore the wallet. Anyone who has that phrase can take the funds.

The implant targets that step. It watches the screen to "take note and transmit the seed phrase you'll be setting up on your ledger," Karpelès wrote on Saturday. He said the implants have "evolved a lot in recent months," becoming harder to spot and easier to install. That means a device can look normal and still be compromised.

"The attacker may decide to steal your assets today, or in a year," Karpelès said. Anyone whose seed phrase was created on an implanted device should make a new one on a safe device and move their assets, he said.

Ledger had confirmed the problem in at least one case. "Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users' devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant," the company's support account wrote. The affected devices were sold through CryptoBilis, a Southeast Asian reseller.

Ledger said CryptoBilis has stopped selling all hardware wallet inventory until the investigation ends. The company said it has "no indication" that its own systems or services were compromised.

Ledger told users who bought from the reseller not to set up their devices. It said those who already have should move their assets to a new Ledger with a new seed phrase. Ledger has not said whether it is aware of any cases in Europe.

The scare surfaced Friday, when Ledger said it was looking into reports of lost funds from Southeast Asian users who bought from CryptoBilis. It asked the reseller to pause all sales and shipments.

On-chain trackers had already started counting losses. Security researcher tanuki42 put the total at more than $72 million, while analyst Specter traced more than $86 million from hundreds of victim wallets.

Blockchain analytics firm Arkham said over $80 million had reportedly been taken across Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Tron (TRX), adding that the cause was unconfirmed. Some of that money has been stopped. tanuki42 said that work with Tether (USDT) and law enforcement had frozen more than $10 million.

title: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana ETFs All in the Red for October
summary: Bitcoin ETFs have seen $386.3 million in net outflows through the first seven trading days of October, while Ethereum funds have now posted nine straight days of losses.
content:
"Uptober" isn't living up to its name for crypto ETFs.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $21.1 million on Friday, according to Decrypt 's ETF tracker. That's a modest bounce after back-to-back outflows of $484.9 million on Wednesday and $244.1 million on Thursday. Even so, the funds are down a net $386.3 million through the first seven trading days of October.

Bitcoin and other crypto asset ETFs allow investors to gain exposure to digital currencies without using crypto exchanges or wallets. These funds track the price of the asset and trade like stocks on a brokerage app. They've been very successful since their launch, and flows in and out of the funds have become a reliable measure of current market sentiment.

The month started strong , with $292.6 million in inflows across Oct. 1 and 2. A $118.8 million inflow on Oct. 6 couldn't offset the selling that followed, and Wednesday's exit was the funds' worst day since June .

That's a sharp reversal from September. After the Senate's failed cloture vote on the Clarity Act triggered heavy outflows in mid-September, Bitcoin ETFs reeled off a nine-session inflow streak worth roughly $3 billion . That run pushed 2026's year-to-date flows back into positive territory.

Ethereum ETFs have fared worse. The funds shed $56.1 million on Friday, extending their outflow streak to nine straight trading days.

They've lost $635 million so far in October and nearly $700 million over the full streak, with the heaviest single-day exit, $201.9 million, coming on Oct. 6. Cumulative net inflows since launch stand at $13.2 billion, and total net assets are $14.5 billion.

Solana ETFs are also in the red for October, though on a much smaller scale. The funds lost $3.8 million on Friday, their fifth straight day of outflows, bringing October's net total to a loss of $24.8 million. Their only inflow this month was $1.3 million on Oct. 2. Cumulative net inflows stand at $137.9 million.

For Bitcoin ETFs, cumulative net inflows since launch total $57.6 billion, and the funds hold $100.6 billion in total net assets, according to Decrypt 's tracker.

Many who share this chart may not fully understand what it measures or how it was constructed. So, can the amount of money in the world really indicate where Bitcoin's price is headed?

M2 measures how much money exists in an economy, including cash, checking accounts, and easily accessible savings like money market funds. The global M2 aggregates these figures across major economies, providing a rough estimate of the total money available worldwide.

The chart that often gets shared compares this global total with Bitcoin's price. However, choosing the money supply line is subjective. Changing the number of weeks in the shift alters the chart's suggested "fair" price for Bitcoin, so the prediction can change whenever the creator adjusts the timeframe.

So, how long might a buyer at the 2025 Bitcoin all-time high expect to wait, and what did previous top buyers experience before recovering their investments?

The first completed cycle peaked on November 30, 2013, at around $1,150. Bitcoin didn't close above that price again until February 23, 2017, about 39 months later.

In 2017, Bitcoin topped out at about $19,800 on December 17, 2017. Bitcoin first closed above $20,000 again on December 16, 2020, after about 36 months. Lower average costs reduce the break-even price, allowing these buyers to recover their investment sooner than those who bought all at once at the top. title: Pokémon Cards Just Crushed Bitcoin, Gold and the S&P 500 With 150% Returns

A halving is a scheduled reduction in the number of new bitcoins miners create and earn. About every four years, the reward for processing transactions is cut in half, so fewer new bitcoins enter circulation each day.

The theory behind the Bitcoin halving is rooted in supply and demand. With less new supply and steady demand, buyers will compete for the limited available coins, which should support the price. title: AI Uncovers XRP Ledger Bug: Is It a Threat or a Defense?
summary: An AI security system just flagged a flaw in the XRP Ledger that human reviewers missed for a decade, and the fix required breaking a decade-long protocol. Now developers across every major crypto network are asking whether AI accelerates their defenses or hands attackers a faster weapon.
content:
AI discovered an XRP Ledger flaw that could have minted 18.45 trillion XRP, a figure 184 times the total supply, threatening its $94 billion market value.

Engineers patched the bug within 3 days, with 80% of validators installing the fix before source code was released to prevent reverse-engineering.

Bitcoin's slow, public upgrade process leaves it far more exposed than XRP during the critical gap between a patch release and full node adoption.

A recent discovery by Veria Labs, a security firm, revealed a major flaw in the XRP Ledger that could have created an astounding 18.45 trillion XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) out of thin air. This amount is more than 184 times the original total supply of 100 billion XRP coins. Veria Labs warned that this bug posed a serious risk to XRP's entire market value, which stood at about $94 billion at the time of the report.

On September 22, 2026, researcher Cayden Liao, together with Veria AI, an artificial intelligence security system, identified this vulnerability. The issue stemmed from a single payment that could buy multiple trading offers at once. A counting error let sellers receive full payment while the buyer was charged almost nothing, creating XRP that never actually existed. Unfortunately, the safety check designed to detect such errors failed because of the same faulty counting code.

RippleX, Ripple's engineering division, said it found no evidence the bug was exploited. Nevertheless, AI's role in pinpointing the bug prompted engineers to revise their approach to releasing fixes for such vulnerabilities.

This revision affects not only XRP holders, with their digital asset trading around $1.39, but also investors in Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), priced at about $82,965, and Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), trading at around $2,501. With that in mind, the question is: Is AI a significant threat to crypto, or is it becoming its best defense?

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

------

AI has identified a flaw that human reviewers missed for a decade, and the researcher who found it was paid to look. Cryptocurrency networks often run bug bounty programs that reward outside researchers for finding vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them. In this case, the bounty system worked as intended, leading to a swift report of the flaw to those able to resolve it.

Engineers reproduced the bug the same day it was reported and patched it within three days. Over 80% of trusted validators, the computers that verify XRP Ledger transactions and ensure accurate records, implemented the patched software on its release day.

The XRP bug adds to a series of long-hidden security weaknesses in the crypto world that AI has helped uncover since July. Several of these discoveries have also involved Bitcoin. For instance, a flaw in the Coldcard wallet, which is a hardware device that secures Bitcoin keys offline, has been linked to the theft of at least 1,367 Bitcoin. Additionally, Core Lightning, software that accelerates Bitcoin transactions, advised operators to disconnect after similar vulnerabilities were discovered.

Although the Coldcard theft is unfortunate, these revelations bring previously concealed issues to light, allowing developers to address them. This suggests AI is bolstering defenses by clearing a backlog of vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.

RippleX engineer Mayukha Vadari shed light on the decision to bypass the XRP Ledger's usual release process for the patch. "Things have changed with AI. You can't just sneak in a critical bug patch in a regular public release process, because you're going to get caught and reverse-engineered right away," Vadari stated.

Attackers can compare new code with the old to pinpoint what has been fixed. Once a patch is public, anyone can do this analysis and see where to target unpatched systems. While this has always been true, machines now perform these comparisons much faster.

In response, XRP Ledger developers released binaries—ready-to-run program files—prior to sharing the underlying source code. This marked the first time a transaction-processing change was issued without passing through the amendment voting process that has governed such updates for over a decade. XRP had this speed advantage because developers could quickly mobilize a small group of trusted validators.

In contrast, Bitcoin lacks a similar system. Its rule changes go through public proposal processes that can take years to finalize, since no node operator can be forced to upgrade. This slow approach safeguards holders from a single group altering the rules, but it also makes the network less agile in fixing issues. Ethereum falls somewhere in between, needing many independent operators to install new software to implement upgrades.

The quick fix to the XRP bug has reignited the debate about transparency. Validators initially ran a program outsiders couldn't inspect, raising concerns about whether the network remains open-source, as many assume. The code was shared later, but holding it back temporarily denied attackers a clear path to unpatched systems.

Moreover, this issue extends to the cryptographic math that underpins every digital wallet. Justin Drake of the Ethereum Foundation has suggested that AI-driven mathematical advancements could pose a more immediate threat to the cryptography securing these networks than quantum computers. Michael Gutkin of Fireblocks countered that researchers have not yet demonstrated a breach of this cryptography. The ongoing debate centers on AI's implications for the development and security of crypto technologies.

For now, AI looks like a net defense. Since July, researchers have reported the flaws it surfaced, and the XRP Ledger fix reached validators before anyone exploited the bug.

The weak spot is the gap between a public patch and enough nodes installing it, and Bitcoin has no small group to upgrade overnight. If attackers exploit a major network inside that gap, AI could start to look like a threat.

title: Why Does Ethereum Fall Harder Than Bitcoin?
summary: Ethereum dropped more than three times harder than Bitcoin last week, yet it also gained far less during the month's rally. Something beyond simple volatility explains why ETH keeps taking the bigger hit without delivering the bigger reward.
content:
Ethereum dropped 7% while Bitcoin fell just 2%, then gained only 1% versus Bitcoin's 6% during the same month's rally.

Ethereum sits 50% below its all-time high and needs a 98% gain to recover, versus Bitcoin's required 52%.

Nine consecutive sessions of Ethereum ETF outflows signal fading institutional demand, adding selling pressure to an already lagging asset.

Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) experienced a decline of 7.0% over the week ending on October 10, 2026, trading at $2,495. In contrast, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) fell only 2.1% during the same period, trading at $82,801. Both cryptocurrencies fell, but when comparing Ethereum vs. Bitcoin, Ethereum's drop was significantly steeper.

Many Ethereum holders know the usual explanation: Ethereum tends to be more volatile, meaning it can fall harder and rise faster when the market shifts. However, data from the past month makes this explanation hard to defend. So, what really causes ETH to drop harder than Bitcoin?

Volatility refers to how much an asset's price swings over time. Traders often say an asset that consistently moves more than another, up or down, is more volatile. Beta is a related term that measures how much an asset tends to move compared to a benchmark. Therefore, a coin with a higher beta than Bitcoin often sees sharper price changes—up or down.

Many crypto enthusiasts hold on to the conventional belief that while volatility carries risks, it also offers rewards. The theory suggests that when Bitcoin rises, Ethereum should rise even more, compensating for deeper losses during downturns.

In this case, Ethereum's drop closely follows the theory. It fell 7.0%, while Bitcoin fell just 2.1%. However, if volatility drives these price movements, the expected rewards should be evident during upside periods.

While both cryptocurrencies gained over the last 30 days, Ethereum rose only 1.3% compared to Bitcoin's 6.4% increase. This time, as the market climbed, ETH lagged significantly behind BTC—contrary to expectations that it would outperform during rallies.

An asset that drops deeper yet gains less isn't offering the higher-volatility payoff. The traditional argument that higher risk leads to higher rewards doesn't hold here, as Ethereum isn't keeping pace with Bitcoin's gains.

Additionally, Ethereum trails Bitcoin even more when you compare each coin's price to its all-time high. Currently, Ethereum is trading 49.5% below its peak of $4,946, meaning it needs a 98.2% increase to return to that level. Bitcoin, on the other hand, is 34.3% below its peak of $126,080, so it only needs a 52.3% gain to recover.

This difference in recovery percentages makes Ethereum harder to recover. For example, if an asset loses half its value, it must double to get back to where it started. Therefore, any additional drop in Ethereum makes it harder to recover than Bitcoin.

The ETH/BTC ratio clearly shows how Ethereum is performing against Bitcoin. It indicates how much Bitcoin one Ethereum can buy, and as of October 10, this ratio stood at 0.03014. A declining ratio means Ethereum is losing its value relative to Bitcoin, and a rising ratio means it is improving.

Furthermore, recent fund flows might be contributing to Ethereum's struggles. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) holding Ethereum—allowing investors to own ETH through standard brokerage accounts—currently have about $15.7 billion in net assets. Data from SoSoValue shows nine consecutive sessions of outflows, meaning more money has been withdrawn than added.

Such a steady outflow could put added pressure on Ethereum's price. However, there's no definitive proof that these outflows directly caused the price movements, as price and fund flows often move in tandem without one directly influencing the other. Additionally, a week or a month may not capture how these coins behaved in earlier recovery phases.

The evidence suggests that yes, Ethereum is taking larger hits without the expected higher gains. The analysis supports the view that Ethereum holders face bigger downturns without the corresponding price spikes that would justify the added risk. While the pattern is evident, the specifics of why this is happening remain unclear.

The ETH/BTC ratio will likely be a key indicator going forward. If it rises above 0.03014 during Bitcoin's next bullish phase and the current streak of ETF outflows reverses, it would show the catch-up behavior Ethereum's supporters promise. However, if the ratio falls while Bitcoin rises, it would suggest that Ethereum's extra volatility isn't rewarding its holders as expected.

title: China Launches National Blockchain As Part Of Wider Plan To Accelerate Expansion Of Digital Economy
summary: Despite having a traditionally conservative stance towards cryptocurrencies, the Chinese Communist Party is moving forward with the construction of a national blockchain network as part of a wider strategy to upgrade Chinese digital infrastructure.
content:
China has unveiled a plan to build a national blockchain network, but the Asian power's planned investment about the technology does not appear to equate to a slackening restrictions on private cryptocurrency trading, which remains banned in mainland China.

The measure was announced in a policy document entitled "Opinions of the CPC Central Committee and the State Council on Developing New Productive Forces." The document was made public by the official Chinese state news agency Xinhua on Friday.

The document made no mention of Bitcoin or other independent cryptocurrencies. Since 2021, Beijing has enacted a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency transactions. The ban extends to foreign cryptocurrency companies who attempt to provide services to people living in mainland China.

China does, however, operate its own sovereign digital currency, the digital yuan. Beijing has recently been encouraging its citizens to increase their use of the digital currency, having recently increased the number of banks authorized to operate digital yuan services from 22 to 30 in August.

China also already invests in blockchain, the technology which enables the existence of cryptocurrencies. China currently has a Blockchain-based Service Network (BSN), a state-backed platform which supports enterprise and government applications but prohibits cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin from operating on its rails.

It is possible, though unconfirmed, that the new system will build on BSN.

The document also called for a more comprehensive integration of the Chinese digital and real economies through the digitalization of the manufacturing industry, the construction of a "national integrated computing power network" and the implementation of the "Eastern Data, Western Computing" project, a mega-infrastructure venture designed to store data generated by China's economically productive and densely populated eastern regions in the less-developed, more sparsely-populated but resource-abundant west of China.

However, officials responsible for the digital transformation are also advised against "abandoning the real economy for the virtual economy, pursuing large-scale and comprehensive development, or creating bubbles."

The two government bodies in charge of implementing and regulating this expanded digitalization will be the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission. These two organizations will likely determine how the new blockchain network is integrated into wider Chinese digital infrastructure.

In response to the news, investor interest in China-linked blockchain project Conflux (CFX) has increased, with CFX steadily increasing since Saturday morning and surging to highs of above $0.07 on Sunday. At 8am EDT on Sunday, Conflux was hovering at $0.066, up more than 26% from Saturday's closing price.

CFX is widely seen as the only regulatory-compliant public blockchain in China because it works closely with state-backed corporations, does not sell unregulated tokens within Chinese borders and its founders have close professional and academic ties to the state-run Tsinghua University.

title: Who Really Owns Bitcoin? Wall Street vs. Ordinary People
summary: Who owns Bitcoin? Individuals hold two-thirds, while Strategy and Metaplanet find holding coins takes cash.
content:
Wall Street is pouring billions into Bitcoin, yet ordinary investors still hold most of the supply. Meanwhile, some of the biggest corporate buyers are spending millions to simply maintain their Bitcoin holdings.

Individuals own an estimated 13.9 million BTC, or 66% of the 21 million coins that will ever exist, according to Bitbo and River data compiled by Motley Fool.

That leaves institutional investors competing for Bitcoin that existing holders may be unwilling to sell.

As of October 9, Bitcoin ETFs held 1.48 million BTC, according to Bitbo. Companies controlled another 1.66 million, while governments held roughly 518,500.

Together, these groups accounted for about 17% of Bitcoin's maximum supply.

Meanwhile, around 1.6 million BTC are estimated to be lost. Another 968,000 sit in wallets linked to Bitcoin's anonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto.

However, ownership is gradually shifting. River data shows individuals sold a net 696,000 BTC in 2025. Businesses, investment funds, and governments purchased nearly one million coins.

If that trend continues, institutions may have to offer higher prices to persuade existing holders to sell.

Holding Bitcoin also comes with costs for companies financing their purchases.

Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, holds roughly 848,000 BTC. Yet its latest disclosure shows it drew $142.5 million from its dollar reserve for dividends and interest during the week ending October 4.

The company also spent $73.7 million buying back preferred shares between October 1 and 4. By comparison, it purchased just 334 BTC for $28.7 million.

Japan's Metaplanet took another approach. According to its October 5 disclosure, it sold 10,000 BTC and repurchased 11,000 during the third quarter to demonstrate liquidity.

The company now holds 44,000 BTC and has limited Bitcoin to 85%–90% of its assets.

With Bitcoin trading near $83,000, institutional demand remains significant. But Strategy's latest spending shows how maintaining a large Bitcoin treasury can compete with buying more coins.

IREN said that engineering teams could decide between two software options -- virtualization for secure multi-tenant environments, or dedicated bare-metal clusters for maximum performance.

IREN, formerly Iris Energy, has mined Bitcoin (BTC) on hydropower in British Columbia since 2019. The company entered the AI space in early 2024 and in March 2025 paused mining expansion to focus on AI cloud.

title: Most Investors Are Wrong About Who Owns the Most Bitcoin. That Misunderstanding Creates a Buying Opportunity.
summary: The people who hold Bitcoin have something that deep-pocketed buyers want.
content:
Ordinary investors, not crypto companies or institutional investors, own most of the world's Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC). Individuals hold about 14 million BTC, or approximately two-thirds of the 21 million BTC that will ever exist, according to River's Bitcoin adoption report for 2026. (River was founded in 2019 to "build the Bitcoin bank of the world.")

The distribution of the coin's supply has been on my mind for years now. But I've only understood very recently that other people's misconceptions about who holds the most of it represent a significant buying opportunity. Let's walk through the logic here.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The biggest single holder of Bitcoin is probably its pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, who disappeared in 2011 and whose identity remains unknown.

Many believe that the wallet addresses that are thought to constitute Satoshi's untouched stash hold 968,000 coins, or 4.6% of all that can exist. An investigation by Cointelegraph in September 2026 found that the estimates of the hoard's exact size range from just under 900,000 to about 1.2 million BTC. Those coins have never moved, and given Satoshi's potentially permanent absence, most people, including yours truly, assume that they never will, as to move them would cause widespread panic that they might be sold.

There are also an estimated 1.6 million coins that are permanently "lost," i.e., inaccessible to their owners. It is with some regret that I report to you that a small quantity of that lost sum was at one point under my control. Regardless, neither that pile nor Satoshi's are likely to re-enter circulation -- I'm certainly never going to find the wallet credentials I was using more than 10 years ago -- which has the effect of shrinking the pool of coins available to everyone else who might want to buy them.

Among the businesses that constitute the biggest potential buyers, Strategy has the most, with 848,000 BTC, or about 4% of the total; every other company combined holds about 3.9%.

As you can see, even exchange-traded funds (ETFs) as a group held just 7.1% of the supply despite being issued by major asset managers. And governments hold about 2.5% of the supply as of early October 2026 -- perhaps only a smidgen of what they could ultimately want to hold over the coming years.

So what does Bitcoin's ownership and distribution indicate?

In short, no single player can dictate its price by manipulating the supply, nor can a major holder manipulate the blockchain's policies, as owning coins does not confer any voting power over the underlying software or the direction that its developers choose to take.

The groups that are the most likely to want far more Bitcoin than they currently own, namely corporations, funds, and governments, today own only a minority of it. In 2025, individual holders sold a net 696,000 BTC while businesses bought 489,000, funds and ETFs 205,000, and governments 135,000, according to data from River. If that trend continues, River projects those three groups could own about 11.7 million BTC, or 56% of the supply cap, by 2036.

To own more, those groups need to buy it from the people who currently hold it by offering a price that the holders find attractive. Given that Bitcoin's supply is mined at a slower and slower rate after each of its halvings, over the long run it is thus quite likely that aspiring buyers will need to bid more and more to secure a portion of the supply. That's why I believe that buying it now will pay off later.

If you have the patience to wait for Bitcoin's slow-moving supply constriction to give way to higher prices, which can take years and is not guaranteed to happen, it's worth buying today and holding while the big accumulators compete for what's left. title: Solana Confirms a Transaction in 200 Milliseconds and Bitcoin Takes 10 Minutes. Does Speed Make a Coin Worth More?
summary: Solana just became 3,000 times faster than Bitcoin at producing blocks, yet its coin lost nearly 8% of its value the same week. The relationship between blockchain speed and price turns out to be far more complicated than it looks.
content:
Solana's 200ms block time is 3,000x faster than Bitcoin's 10-minute pace, yet SOL dropped 7.9% the week the upgrade went live.

Block speed and finality are different metrics, and it is worth noting that XRP already settles payments in 3 to 5 seconds while Solana's Alpenglow finality update isn't live yet.

Bitcoin gained 29% over 90 days with zero speed changes, suggesting that market momentum rather than technical upgrades is what drives crypto prices.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) has recently improved its performance by creating a new block every 200 milliseconds, compared to Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), which produces a block approximately every 10 minutes. On paper, this means Solana's block speed is about 3,000 times faster than Bitcoin's. Bitcoin users generally wait for six confirmations, making the total wait time roughly an hour before they consider a payment secure.

Solana's network made the switch to 200-millisecond block times on October 9, 2026. However, despite this enhancement, Solana's price stands at around $110 as of October 10—a 7.9% decrease over the past week, making it the worst-performing major coin during that period. This raises the question: does speed truly make a coin more valuable?

A blockchain is a shared digital ledger that groups transactions into blocks, which are added one at a time. Block time refers to how frequently new blocks are added to the chain. Solana reduced its block time step by step: from 400 milliseconds to 350 milliseconds on August 21, then to 300, 250, and finally 200 milliseconds on October 9.

------

------

However, merchants and exchanges care more than speed about finality—the point at which a payment can no longer be reversed. A block might be produced quickly, but it could still be reversible for some time. In Bitcoin's case, each confirmation adds another block onto the one containing a transaction, making a reversal increasingly difficult with every confirmation.

Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) produces a block roughly every 12 seconds and reaches finality in about 13 minutes. Meanwhile, the XRP Ledger, which supports XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), completes payments in 3 to 5 seconds. Solana's next planned update, Alpenglow, aims for finality of around 150 milliseconds, but this feature isn't live yet.

These numbers don't tell the whole story. Each network balances speed against costs and the number of computers required to verify each block. Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin's creator, deliberately set its 10-minute pace to give computers around the world ample time to receive and agree on each block. This slower pace reflects different priorities rather than a flaw in the system.

Solana's network officially went live with its fastest update on October 9, yet the coin's price fell 7.9% over the past week, more than any other major coin. As the final speed upgrade date approached, holders appeared to sell off their assets.

However, looking at longer time frames is more favorable for Solana holders. The coin has appreciated by 8.7% over the past 30 days, 43% over 60 days, and 42% over 90 days. These gains include the first speed enhancement from August 21 and Solana's September rally, which supporters may cite as evidence of the upgrade's benefits.

On the flip side, Bitcoin has seen a 29% increase over the same 90-day span, despite not changing its block time. This suggests a broader market rally, indicating that Solana's larger percentage gains may reflect the typical swings seen in smaller, more volatile coins during market uptrends, rather than solely its faster block production.

Currently, Solana trades about 63% below its all-time high of $293, reached in January 2025, and needs a 167% increase to regain that peak. Although the network is operating at its fastest, the coin's price remains far below its peak.

In conclusion, speed alone does not necessarily increase a coin's value. Solana's recent upgrades haven't translated into a price increase, showing that technology improvements must attract real users and fees to boost demand.

Faster transaction speeds are an impressive technical feat and can create a competitive edge, but they don't, by themselves, guarantee a price rise. Until Solana's Alpenglow update is fully operational and the network attracts more users, the impact of its speed enhancements on SOL's value remains uncertain.

The true test will be whether Solana's fees and transaction activity increase significantly from their pre-October 9 levels once Alpenglow is live. If they do, we could see the demand for SOL reflect positively in its price.

title: Whales Bought 15,000 Bitcoin in Three Days While MARA Sold $81 Million. Who Has It Right?
summary: Bitcoin whales poured over a billion dollars into the market right after a sharp decline, while one of the biggest mining companies quietly cashed out. Their opposing moves point to very different views on where Bitcoin goes from here.
content:
Whales accumulated 15,000 BTC worth $1.24 billion after Bitcoin's October 7 drop, while smaller wallets shed holdings into the decline.

MARA sold 996 BTC for $81 million to fund debt repayment, shrinking total borrowings from $3.6 billion to $2.4 billion.

Bitcoin trades 17% above MARA's first-half average sale price of $70,631, showing its selling tracks financing schedules, not price forecasts.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

In the days after the October 7 decline, Bitcoin whales—those with medium and large wallets—bought about 15,000 Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), worth around $1.24 billion at current prices, according to analyst Ali Martinez. In contrast, on October 9, MARA Holdings ( NASDAQ:MARA ), one of the largest publicly traded Bitcoin mining companies, sold 996 BTC, valued at about $81 million, during the same period.

As of October 10, Bitcoin is trading at $82,801, down 2.1% over the week and 34.3% below its all-time high of $126,080. This creates a clear dichotomy: one group bought the dip, while a major miner decided to sell. So which perspective is more accurate for Bitcoin's future, and is MARA truly making a statement about its price?

Martinez's findings indicate that medium and large wallets accumulated about 15,000 BTC, along with adding over 166,000 Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) and around 45 million XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) during the same three days, while smaller wallets continued to sell. Based on today's prices, these purchases amount to about $1.24 billion in Bitcoin, $414 million in Ether at $2,495, and $63 million in XRP at $1.40.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

However, wallet data categorizes blockchain addresses by the amount of cryptocurrency they hold without revealing their owners. This means a single individual or company can control multiple wallets, and an exchange moving coins between its accounts can look like a large buyer accumulating coins. Additionally, Martinez did not specify the data provider or clarify the thresholds for categorizing wallets as "medium" or "large," making it difficult for readers to verify whether exchange wallets were excluded from the analysis.

Nonetheless, the trend is clear: large wallets added coins while smaller wallets shed them during the market drop.

Data also show that spot Bitcoin ETFs experienced a notable shift. Investors withdrew $487 million on October 7 and $244 million on October 8, then saw a modest $21 million inflow on October 9, according to SoSoValue. This small inflow coincided with whales' buying activity but remains minor compared with the heavier outflows seen earlier.

Bitcoin miners run specialized computers to secure the Bitcoin network and earn new coins as a reward. MARA's October 9 sale of 996 BTC represented 2.8% of its total holdings, which currently stand at 35,303 BTC valued at about $2.92 billion. MARA's holdings have decreased by 34.4% since it held 53,822 BTC on December 31, 2025.

In the first half of 2026, MARA sold around 23,093 BTC for about $1.63 billion, averaging approximately $70,631 per coin. This total includes selling 20,880 coins for about $1.5 billion in the first quarter and 2,213 coins at an average price of $73,078 in the second quarter. The company has stated its intention to "continue to monetize bitcoin opportunistically to fund operations and capital projects," using the cash for operating expenses, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

This selling strategy has reduced MARA's total debt from $3.6 billion to about $2.4 billion, including partial repayment of $912.8 million in convertible notes, a $350 million credit line, and the buyback of nearly $1 billion in 0% convertible notes. Convertible notes are loans that can be converted into shares later, so eliminating them reduces both debt and potential future stock issuance.

Shareholders have welcomed this approach. For instance, on March 26, MARA's stock surged 10% after a $1.1 billion Bitcoin sale funded a debt buyback, successfully retiring some of the company's borrowings early. Bitcoin is currently trading about 13.3% above MARA's average sale price from the second quarter and 17.2% above the first-half average, suggesting a selling strategy tied more to financing schedules than to price predictions.

It appears that only the whales are making a prediction about Bitcoin's price. MARA seems more focused on repairing its financial position, and the 996 BTC sale aligns with its debt obligations. While accumulation data from larger wallets suggests a positive move, the unnamed wallets used in the analysis and the single day of fund inflows do not definitively prove the whales' outlook is correct. The information merely supports a narrower conclusion: larger holders acquired the Bitcoin that smaller holders sold after the October 7 drop.

MARA's upcoming holdings update could provide more clarity. If the company's stack shrinks further while total debt stays around $2.4 billion, it would suggest sales are no longer aimed at paying down debt, warranting a reevaluation of whether MARA is making a price prediction. Until more data comes in, MARA's selling appears to be a strategic move aligned with financial responsibilities, while Bitcoin's direction will largely depend on continued whale buying and ETF inflows.

title: Eight Altcoins Have Surged Three Times More Than Bitcoin in 30 Days. Is Altcoin Season Here, or Is This Just a Momentary Uptick?
summary: Eight altcoins are trouncing Bitcoin's returns over the past month, sparking talk of a long-awaited altcoin season. But a closer look at the weekly numbers and a key market index tells a very different story.
content:
NEAR Protocol surged 121% in 30 days, leading eight altcoins that each outperformed Bitcoin's 6.4% gain by at least three times.

Six of the eight outperforming altcoins have already reversed lower this week, with Uniswap erasing nearly half its monthly gains in seven days.

The Altcoin Season Index sits at 51, well below the 75 threshold required to declare a season, and no true altcoin season has occurred in 379 days.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Over the last 30 days, eight altcoins have seen returns at least three times greater than Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC). This impressive performance has led traders to wonder if we are entering an altcoin season. Leading the charge is NEAR Protocol (CRYPTO:NEAR), which has surged 121%, far outpacing Bitcoin's 6.4% gain over the same period.

The other seven coins making waves are Sui (CRYPTO:SUI), Aave (CRYPTO:AAVE), Avalanche (CRYPTO:AVAX), Uniswap (CRYPTO:UNI), Litecoin (CRYPTO:LTC), Hedera (CRYPTO:HBAR), and Cardano (CRYPTO:ADA). Even Cardano, at the bottom of the list, boasts a respectable 20% gain—more than three times Bitcoin's increase.

Traders often see such a leaderboard as potential evidence of an altcoin season. However, six of these eight coins have declined over the past week, and the Altcoin Season Index still hasn't reached its critical levels. So, the question remains: Are we truly starting an altcoin season, or is this just a short-term bounce?

Altcoins are any cryptocurrencies aside from Bitcoin, and "altcoin season" describes a phase when traders shift funds out of Bitcoin and into smaller coins, leading to substantial gains for most altcoins. Conversely, a "Bitcoin season" occurs when Bitcoin outperforms the majority of the market.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

------

The Altcoin Season Index formalizes this concept, declaring altcoin season only when 75% of the 50 largest coins outperform Bitcoin over a 90-day timeframe. As of October 10, 2026, the index is at 51, indicating that we are "not in Altcoin Season." Remarkably, it has been 379 days since the last altcoin season and 39 days since the last Bitcoin season.

CoinMarketCap's version of the index showed 61 on October 1, which also falls short of the 75 threshold. Both indexes intentionally measure a 90-day period to prevent a single strong month from prematurely indicating a season.

Only NEAR (up 13%) and Cardano (up 3%) have maintained an upward trend over the past week. Meanwhile, the other six coins have experienced declines.

This quick unwind points to a temporary bounce, since the rotation reversed within the same month it began. In a lasting trend, altcoins typically continue to outperform Bitcoin week after week, but many of these coins stopped that trend before the month ended.

Still, three reasons suggest the possibility of a longer rally. First, Bitcoin also dropped 2% over the past week, suggesting the altcoin declines occurred during a broader market dip rather than a rotation back into Bitcoin. Two, two of the eight coins are still climbing. Lastly, a one-week period is a brief timeframe for assessing market trends. Furthermore, the impressive 30-day gains took place without any clear news driving them.

A bigger concern for these coins is how far they fell before this recent recovery. Each of the eight coins is trading substantially below its all-time high. For instance, Avalanche is down 93% from its peak, while Cardano is down 92%, and Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap have each fallen between 83% and 85%.

Sui is down 79%, and NEAR and Aave are both down 74%. In contrast, Bitcoin is down 34% from its peak.

A coin that has lost more than 90% can still rise substantially and linger far below previous price levels, because the gain starts from a much lower base. For example, Cardano would need to increase roughly 12 times its current value to reclaim its prior record, making a 20% monthly gain seem minimal in that context. A leaderboard ranking by percentage gains tends to favor coins that faced the biggest declines, as they rebound from lower starting points.

The current 30-day outlook suggests the start of an altcoin season, but the evidence leans toward a bounce. Six of the eight coins have already turned negative over the past week, and the Altcoin Season Index stands at 51, far below the 75 threshold needed for a season call. A genuine altcoin season requires sustained outperformance across the 50 largest coins over several months, and a handful of coins showing short-term gains does not provide enough support for such a declaration.

For holders of these coins, the index serves as a vital indicator. A reading of 75 or higher would contradict the bounce scenario and signal the first altcoin season in 379 days. title: Could $1,000 Invested in Bitcoin Help You Retire a Millionaire?
summary: At one time, Bitcoin had 1,000x upside potential. But is that still the case?
content:
Since its launch back in 2009, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) has gained an absolutely incredible 134,900,000%. For good reason, it has acquired a reputation as a potential millionaire maker.

But that was then. The days of Bitcoin's stratospheric annual returns may be coming to an end. As institutional investors pile into Bitcoin , it is increasingly behaving like a high-beta tech stock. Thus, it's going to be a lot harder to turn $1,000 into $1 million.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The math behind any potential millionaire-maker coin is relatively simple, at least when the contemplated investment is small. The only way to turn $1,000 into $1 million is if the coin has 1,000x upside potential.

At one time, Bitcoin had this type of upside potential. It's how the cryptocurrency went from a $1 price tag to a $1,000 value, and from $100 to $100,000.

But is that still the case? From a current price of $85,000, Bitcoin would need to skyrocket to $85 million. That's preposterous, and well beyond the price target of even the most bullish Bitcoin investor. Take Michael Saylor of Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR), for example. He thinks Bitcoin is headed to $21 million in 21 years .

Just think of the math involved if Bitcoin were to hit a price of $85 million. Right now, Bitcoin has a market cap of $1.7 trillion. So 1,000x upside implies a future market cap measured in the quadrillions, not the trillions. That simply does not make any kind of sense.

Or, think of it another way. Bitcoin at a price of $85 million would be worth nearly 1,000 times the current value of Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX). Right now, SpaceX has a market cap of $2.2 trillion.

That being said, it is possible to think of a few alternative paths to millionaire status. For example, investors could dabble in Bitcoin derivatives (such as perpetual futures) or Bitcoin prediction market contracts.

In both cases, investors can take on tremendous leverage, setting up the opportunity for massive gains (as well as crushing losses). On Kalshi, for example, retail investors can take on 6.8x leverage when trading Bitcoin perpetual futures.

So, in this hypothetical scenario, an investor might be able to transform $1,000 into $10,000 using leverage. Then, that money could be plowed into the spot crypto market. In this scenario, Bitcoin would only need 100x upside potential. That's still asking a lot of Bitcoin, but at least the numbers start to make at least a little more sense.

Long story short, the most likely path to millionaire status is by spotting the potential of a cryptocurrency investment early, long before anyone else thinks it's valuable.

That was the case with Bitcoin in the early days, when nobody could imagine it even reaching $10, $100, or $1,000. Now it's worth $85,000.

summary: A couple of popular institutional trades are driving much of the purchasing activity.
content:
U.S. spot Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) received about $2.6 billion in capital inflows over the three-week period ending on Oct. 2. To most Bitcoin holders, that's good news, as it builds on the trend of Bitcoin ETFs seeing regular flowing in instead of flowing out, even though the coin remains about 32% below its October 2025 peak.

However, there's more to the story. Here's the fuller context for what's driving Bitcoin and its ETFs upward as I write this in October 2026.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Hedge funds and institutional investors have a few different purposes for Bitcoin ETF shares than most individual investors do. And there's at least one piece of evidence suggesting that hedge funds are responsible for at least some of the inflows into Bitcoin ETFs.

In what's called a basis trade: A hedge fund purchases Bitcoin ETF shares and simultaneously sells Bitcoin futures contracts for later delivery at higher prices, enabling it to capture the gap between the two as prices converge. Such trades can be performed profitably whether Bitcoin itself rises or falls, and CoinShares' James Butterfill told Cointelegraph in September that "at the moment the basis trade has an attractive yield at 6%..." For a player with a lot of capital, that could be a very meaningful gain.

The catch is that the capital used in the basis trade tends to leave for greener pastures when the spread between the ETF price and the futures contract price shrinks to be too small to be worth executing the trade.

In Q1 of 2026, hedge funds cut their ETF holdings by 39%, per an analysis of regulatory filings performed by CoinShares. Professional investors owned just 20.8% of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF assets in Q1 2026, and financial advisors, who tend to make long-term allocations, held 58% of that share.

Per the on-chain data, large private wallets are among Bitcoin's buyers at the moment. Wallets holding between 100 and 1,000 BTC added 113,950 BTC from mid-July to late September 2026, per data from Santiment.

Similar to the basis trade, another likely motive for the ongoing purchasing is what's called the debasement trade. The debasement trade is a bet that heavy U.S. government borrowing and/or money printing will erode the dollar's value, thereby driving investors to buy inflation-resistant assets, including Bitcoin, which might eventually prove to be one.

Many investors date the debasement trade's revival to mid-August 2026, when the Treasury Department announced that it would double its buybacks of long-dated sovereign debt, and then later tripled them. Bitcoin went on to climb by about 35% from that point in mid-August to early October.

So Bitcoin's ETF inflows are being driven in large part by deep-pocketed investors with a lot of capital that they want to monetize and protect. If that group becomes more fearful, expect the inflows to accelerate.

title: Fidelity’s Global Macro Director Jurrien Timmer Says Bitcoin Has Bottomed And Should Beat Gold Here On
summary: Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer expects Bitcoin to outperform gold from here, even as he saw gold's fair value near $5,000 and rising.
content:
Jurrien Timmer said Bitcoin has bottomed, and pointed to its double bottom around 58,000 to 60,000 and its move back above $80,000.

Timmer said his cycle model had pointed to a peak near $150,000, but Bitcoin topped near $126,000 instead.

Timmer warned that the 10-year Treasury yield near 5.3% is pressuring stocks into a "stealth correction," making the case for diversifying into gold, Bitcoin and commodities.

Bitcoin (BTC) has bottomed and should outperform gold from here, according to Fidelity Investments' Jurrien Timmer. Timmer stated that Bitcoin ended a mild bear market, and its rise above $80,000 confirmed a double bottom, indicating that the price may have found support.

Timmer, the firm's director of global macro, made the call during an appearance on The Compound & Friends podcast on Friday. Timmer said "60K is a level that I'm going to buy and it went to 58," and that is a chart pattern in which a price tests a low twice and holds. He said the price looked right earlier this year, but the timing did not. Bitcoin's winters have tended to last 9 to 12 months, he said. Traders often read it as a sign that a downtrend is over.

He expects both Bitcoin and gold to rally. He said there's more room for Bitcoin to run. "Bitcoin is going to go up more," he said.

His cycle model had pointed to a peak close to $150,000 last year, said Timmer. He said Bitcoin topped out at about $126,000. The model plots time and price on logarithmic scales, compressing large moves to make it easier to compare patterns. Each winter is shorter than the previous one, he said. "It's a maturing asset, right? So, it's going to moon less and it's going to swoon less," he said.

After Bitcoin's peak, speculators moved out of Bitcoin into gold, Timmer said. That took gold to around $5,600, he said. His model of the global money supply indicates gold should not have risen above $4,800, he said. Fair value is about $5,000 and climbing, he added. Bitcoin priced in gold shows a double bottom too, he said.

Timmer's take comes with a warning on bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield is around 5.3%, he said. He said rising yields are putting pressure on stocks and creating what he called a stealth correction.

Timmer said gold, Bitcoin and commodities can help diversify portfolios when stocks and bonds fall together. However, he warned that some of these assets could become more closely correlated with equities, limiting their diversification benefits.
